faqs.question: How long does a Diwali rangoli take to make?
faqs.answer: From 15 minutes to about two hours, depending on size. A trail of Lakshmi footprints in rice paste takes about 15 minutes and needs only 2 tablespoons of soaked, ground rice. If you have half an hour, add the triangle-grid diya, which needs four rows of dots and two colours.

faqs.question: How do I make the rice paste for an alpana-style rangoli?
faqs.answer: Soak about 2 tablespoons of rice for two hours, then grind it with a little water until it is thin and milky. Dip a small cotton rag in it and let the paste run down your finger as you draw; it dries white.

faqs.question: Can I make a rangoli with only rice flour and no colours?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the kolam tradition of Tamil Nadu mostly does. A white single-line kolam on a 4-by-5 dot grid takes about 35 minutes and 200 g of rice flour, and it reads well on a dark floor.

faqs.question: How do I draw a perfect circle for a rangoli without a compass?
faqs.answer: Tie chalk to a string, hold the other end at the centre with your thumb and walk the chalk round. The same string also divides the circle: stepped around the rim, its length marks six equal points.

faqs.question: Why does my kolam line keep ending up as two separate loops?
faqs.answer: Your dot grid's sides share a factor. For the lattice kolam, a 2015 paper in the journal Forma gives the loop count as the greatest common divisor of the two sides, so a 4-by-6 grid makes 2 loops while a 4-by-5 grid makes one.

faqs.question: How do I make red rangoli colour at home?
faqs.answer: Mix a pinch of slaked lime (chuna) into haldi with a few drops of water; the alkali turns the yellow to orange-red, which is how kumkum is traditionally made. Use a spoon rather than your fingers, because chuna irritates skin.

faqs.question: How do I keep a rangoli intact for all five days of Diwali?
faqs.answer: Draw the outline in wet rice paste, which dries hard and lasts several days, and redraw only the coloured fill each morning. Dry powder rarely survives more than one sweep.

faqs.question: Which day should I draw the rangoli for Diwali 2027?
faqs.answer: The main design goes down for Lakshmi Puja on Friday 29 October 2027. Many homes start a smaller one at the door on Dhanteras, Wednesday 27 October, and keep it going to Bhai Dooj on 31 October.

faqs.question: Is a rangoli the same thing as a kolam or an alpana?
faqs.answer: They are regional forms of the same floor art. NIOS lists Kolam in Tamil Nadu, Alpana in Bengal, Mandana in Rajasthan, Aripan in Bihar and Muggu in Andhra Pradesh; kolam is usually dot-based white line work, alpana a white rice-paste painting.

faqs.question: Can I draw a rangoli on glossy tiles in a flat?
faqs.answer: Yes, but dry powder slides and scatters on polished tiles. Lay the outline in rice paste or chalk first, keep the design to a 2-foot size away from the main walkway, and fill it last.

faqs.question: Does SubhSandesh have a rangoli design tool?
faqs.answer: No. Its Diwali greeting page includes one scene where the recipient colours a rangoli until your initials glow, but it cannot design, plan or print a floor rangoli. It is for wishing one person who is not with you.

# Diwali Rangoli Designs You Can Finish Before the Puja Starts

The Diwali rangoli designs below are six original patterns written as steps, not photos, and graded by size, time and skill: a Lakshmi footprint trail takes about 15 minutes, an 18-inch diya about 30, and a 4-foot courtyard ring two hours with a helper. Pick by the time you really have. SubhSandesh's nearest festival data says most people do festival things late: of 89 greeting pages built for Raksha Bandhan 2026, 49.4% were made on the festival day itself and 27.0% the day before. That is a different festival and a small sample, but if your rangoli follows the same pattern it gets drawn on Diwali morning, Friday 29 October 2027, with the puja hours away. This page covers the six designs, a materials table with quantities, how to make red from haldi, and the kolam mathematics that tells you whether a line will close.

## What makes a Diwali rangoli different from an everyday kolam?

A Diwali rangoli is a floor design drawn at the threshold or puja spot for Lakshmi Puja, usually larger and more coloured than the daily kolam, and often carrying Lakshmi's footprints walking into the house. The craft is the same one India knows by a dozen names. The [National Institute of Open Schooling's rangoli lesson](https://www.nios.ac.in/media/documents/244_Folk_art/Folk_Art_Practical_L-5.pdf) lists Chawk Purna in Uttar Pradesh, Mandana in Rajasthan, Aripan in Bihar, Alpana in Bengal, Kolam in Tamil Nadu and Muggu in Andhra Pradesh.

What changes at Diwali is the motif. The NIOS [Alpana lesson](https://www.nios.ac.in/media/documents/244_Folk_art/Folk_Art_Practical_L-6.pdf) says Lakshmi's footprints are a must during Lakshmi Puja and always point towards the inside of the house, signifying the goddess entering. Get that direction right and the simplest design is correct.

## Six Diwali rangoli designs, graded from 15 minutes to 2 hours

Every design lists size, time, skill and material, in that order, and time comes second for a reason: in the same Raksha Bandhan 2026 analogue (n = 89), 86.1% of the pages finished in time were built within 24 hours of the festival. Times are our estimates for one person on a smooth floor, including clean-up of mistakes; powder figures assume a filled design and run about 100–150 g per square foot.

### 1. Lakshmi charan trail in rice paste

**Size:** door to puja spot, about six pairs. **Time:** 15 minutes. **Skill:** beginner. **Material:** 2 tablespoons of rice. Soak the rice for two hours, grind it with a little water to a thin milky paste, and soak a cotton rag in it. For each foot, press the side of your closed fist for the sole and dab five fingertip dots for the toes. Walk the pairs inward, toes pointing into the house, a stride apart. It dries white and holds better than dry powder underfoot.

### 2. Triangle-grid diya

**Size:** 18 inches wide. **Time:** 30 minutes. **Skill:** beginner. **Material:** 250 g white powder, 100 g orange. Lay four centred rows of dots, 7, 5, 3 and 1 from the bottom, 2 inches apart. Join the bottom row's ends to the 5-dot row's ends in a shallow curve for the bowl, and run a straight rim along the 5-dot row. For the flame, stack three chevrons point-up above the top dot, each smaller than the last. Fill the bowl orange and the chevrons yellow, red, yellow.

### 3. Wave-and-dot threshold border

**Size:** 3 feet by 6 inches. **Time:** 40 minutes. **Skill:** intermediate. **Material:** 300 g across three colours. Run two parallel chalk lines 6 inches apart along the step. Put a dot every 3 inches down the middle, then draw one continuous S-wave weaving above and below alternate dots, and a second wave in the mirror rhythm so the two cross between dots. Fill the eye-shaped gaps red, the outer scallops yellow, and dot white along both edges. It fits a doorstep where a circle would hit the frame.

### 4. Six-petal string-compass flower

**Size:** 30-inch circle. **Time:** 55 minutes. **Skill:** intermediate. **Material:** 600 g across four shades. Tie chalk to a 7.5-inch string, hold the other end at the centre and draw a circle. Without changing the string, step its length around the rim: it marks exactly six equal points, because a chord equal to the radius cuts off 60 degrees. Centre the same string on each point and draw an arc inside the circle; six overlapping petals appear. Ring it with a second circle at 15 inches and shade petals light to dark.

### 5. Single-line lattice kolam on a 4-by-5 grid

**Size:** 2 feet by 2.5 feet. **Time:** 35 minutes. **Skill:** intermediate. **Material:** 200 g rice flour, no colour. Put down 4 rows of 5 dots, 5 inches apart. Start the line in any gap at the edge and travel diagonally between dots; when you hit the outside, curl round the edge dot and head back diagonally. Keep going until you return to your start. On this grid the line closes as one unbroken loop, for a reason explained in the geometry section below.

### 6. Deep-mala courtyard ring

**Size:** 4-foot circle. **Time:** 2 hours with two people. **Skill:** advanced. **Material:** 1.2–1.5 kg. Draw the outer circle with a 24-inch string and step it round the rim, as in design 4, for six points. Halve each gap to get 12 points and draw a small design-2 diya at each. Put design 4 in the centre and lay a band of one repeated leaf motif between centre and rim.

## Rangoli materials compared: flour, powder, petals, paste and haldi

The material decides how long the design survives feet and the first sweep, so choose it first. The table compares five options for a 2-foot design; quantities and durations are our estimates, and costs are left out because they vary sharply by city in Diwali week.

| Material | Best for | Needed for a 2-ft design | Lasts on a swept floor |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rice flour (dry) | Outlines, kolam lines | 150–250 g | Until first sweep, about 1 day |
| Coloured rangoli powder | Filled designs 2, 3, 4 | 400–600 g | 1–2 days if undisturbed |
| Rice paste (wet) | Lakshmi footprints, alpana | 2–4 tablespoons of rice | 3–5 days, dries hard |
| Marigold and rose petals | Borders, quick fills | 300–500 g | 1 day before wilting |
| Haldi, kumkum, geru | Natural accent colours | 50–100 g each | 1–2 days, may stain grout |

If the design must last all five days from Dhanteras on 27 October to Bhai Dooj on 31 October 2027, use rice paste for the outline and redraw only the colour each morning.

## Natural colours: making red from haldi and chuna

You can colour a rangoli without a packet. The NIOS rangoli lesson names rice paste, powder made from leaves, charcoal, burnt soil and wood sawdust as the traditional ingredients, with sindoor and haldi added for colour; chemical colours, it says, are a modern variation. The Alpana lesson adds red soil (geru) and yellow soil.

The useful trick is red. A [2021 study in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC8272479) describes kumkum as prepared by mixing turmeric with slaked lime, the alkaline chuna sold for paan, and used a 2:1 ratio of turmeric to lime in its preparation. At home, a pinch of chuna stirred into haldi with a few drops of water turns it from yellow to deep orange-red. Chuna is caustic, so mix it with a spoon, not your fingers, and keep it away from children's hands.

That gives a natural palette of six: white rice, yellow haldi, red haldi-plus-chuna, brown geru, black charcoal and green powdered leaves. Expect softer shades than shop powder.

## The geometry: why some kolam lines never close

A [2015 paper in the journal Forma](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/forma/30/1/30_9/_article/-char/en) by Shojiro Nagata treats the kolam line as a knot and states the rule for the lattice kolam: on an N-by-M dot array, the number of separate loops equals the greatest common divisor of N and M. That is why design 5 works. A 4-by-5 grid shares no factor, so you get 1 loop; a 4-by-6 grid gives 2, and a 6-by-6 grid gives 6 separate loops.

So if you want one continuous line, choose grid sides with no common factor: 3 by 4, 4 by 5, 5 by 6 or 5 by 7. An [essay on kambi kolam by designer Anu Reddy (November 2023)](https://alpaca.pubpub.org/pub/xywz3ebv/release/1) describes the hand method behind it: the line goes around each dot once and only once, and the maker keeps looking ahead to the next dot to decide which way the line turns.

Size does not have to mean complexity. A [2021 study in Evolutionary Human Sciences](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC10427318) analysed 3,139 kolam drawn by 192 women in the Kodaikanal region of Tamil Nadu and found complexity, measured as information entropy, stayed roughly constant from small drawings to large ones. Our reading for design 6: when a rangoli grows, repeat two or three motifs evenly instead of adding new ones.

## When a rangoli is the wrong way to wish someone

A rangoli only reaches people who walk past your door; for a sister in Pune or a friend in Toronto it is a photo at best. SubhSandesh does not design rangolis. It makes greeting pages, which matter here only for the person you cannot share a threshold with.

Its [interactive Diwali card on SubhSandesh](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-diwali) has one rangoli scene: the person you send it to colours a rangoli until your initials glow in the middle, alongside a diya at their door, sky lanterns holding up to six of your photos and a letter in a red-and-gold liffafa. It is not a pattern maker and cannot print or plan a floor design. Across SubhSandesh, 48.3% of shared pages are opened on a phone, so the scene is sized for a phone screen, not a courtyard.

If you have drawn a rangoli you are proud of, photograph it from directly above and turn it into a [photo jigsaw that reveals your letter piece by piece](https://subhsandesh.in/photo-puzzle). That sends the real 55-minute flower to someone who will never stand at your door.

- NIOS Folk Art (244), Practical Lesson 6: [Alpana](https://www.nios.ac.in/media/documents/244_Folk_art/Folk_Art_Practical_L-6.pdf).
- Lavanya A. et al., [Natural stain (Kumkum) formulated by the extract of Curcuma aromatica and slaked lime](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC8272479), Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology, May 2021.
- Nagata S., [How Many Loops Kolam Loop Pattern Consists of](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/forma/30/1/30_9/_article/-char/en), Forma 30(1), 2015.
- Reddy A., [Kambi Kolam as Algorithmic Pattern](https://alpaca.pubpub.org/pub/xywz3ebv/release/1), Alpaca Salon, 27 November 2023.
- Tran N.-H. et al., [Entropy trade-offs in artistic design: A case study of Tamil kolam](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC10427318), Evolutionary Human Sciences, 2021.
